intent.statement: Disk Steward treats build output, shared developer caches and repositories as single evidence objects rather than per-file rows, so a real-sized scope finishes scanning inside the configured limit and the user sees where reclaimable space actually is, with a stated rebuild path and an explicit review step before anything is removed.

success_evidence.description: A scan of a scope containing a million files behind objects completes and publishes current state inside the configured storage limit.
A directory is classified as build output only on project evidence; a directory tracked by its repository is never classified as an artifact.
Each object reports size, file count, owning project, detection confidence, measurement freshness and rebuild command, and stores no per-file rows inside itself.
Shared tool-owned caches outside watched roots are discoverable as objects under the same contract, only after explicit opt-in.
A repository is measured as one object and is never offered as a cleanup candidate.
An existing installation migrates by collapsing per-file rows into objects without losing unrelated evidence, with a rehearsed rollback.
Objects are ranked by reclaim value from recorded inputs, and cleanup candidates always require human review.

constraints: Never delete, move or modify any user file; cleanup remains a reviewed, user-initiated action outside this intent.
Never open the user's live evidence database from tests or measurements; use captured copies in isolated snapshots.
Classification must not execute project tooling or build commands.
Preserve the closed reliability plan's bounded-resource, isolation and recovery guarantees.
No signing, notarization, installation or Homebrew publication inside this intent.
non_goals: Automatic or unattended deletion of any object.
Per-file provenance inside a classified object.
Rebuilding or restoring artifacts on the user's behalf.

assumptions.statement: Project markers plus git ignore and tracking classify enough of a real corpus to be useful, with a manifest-anchored fallback where no repository exists.
Recursive sizing of objects on a bounded schedule, driven by file-system events, stays inside the existing resource budgets.
Collapsing existing per-file rows into objects is migratable and reversible on a real installed store.

acceptance_criteria.description: The contract states the object row shape, the confidence vocabulary, the never-classify and never-offer rules, sizing and staleness semantics, and the reversible migration requirement, each traceable to a test or an inspection.

checks.command: consistency check against the closed plan's safety contract
checks.notes: Section 9 inherits bounded resources, test isolation, conflict-safe configuration and recoverable migration from docs/reliability/evidence/CONTRACT-510/safety-contract.md without re-proving them.

acceptance_evidence.reference: docs/reliability/evidence/CONTRACT-601/object-contract.md sections 2 to 8: row shape, confidence vocabulary, never-classify and never-offer rules, sizing and staleness, reversible migration, each naming its proving task.

evidence: Sections 2 to 8 state the row shape, the confidence vocabulary, the never-classify and never-offer rules, sizing and staleness semantics, and the reversible migration requirement.

nodes.title: Validate object detection rules on a real corpus
nodes.summary: Measure how project markers, git ignore and git tracking classify candidate object directories on the maintainer corpus and on fixtures, and record where each rule is decisive, where it is unavailable, and what it would misclassify.

acceptance_criteria.description: Classification of every candidate directory in the corpus is reported with its deciding rule; directories tracked by git are never classified as artifacts; the share of candidates outside any repository is measured and the fallback rule for them is chosen from that evidence.

required_evidence.description: Counts per deciding rule, false-positive examples, and the fixture set that reproduces them.

commands: python3 Scripts/Testing/<measurement script> (read-only over a corpus copy)
deliverables: Detection-rule measurement note with per-rule counts and misclassification examples
non_goals: Deleting or modifying any measured file

checks.notes: 8 of 8 fixture cases classify by the expected rule, including a tracked lookalike refused as source, a virtualenv with a non-standard name, a stray __pycache__ and nested node_modules collapsed to the outermost match.
First rule set: 1,448 of 2,615 output candidates unresolved because a parent manifest resolved only 20 outside repositories.

checks.command: same tool after adding self-marker and content evidence, --output .../corpus-2
checks.notes: Unresolved fell to 27; 1518 objects collapse 929,727 files and 70.2 GB; 29 tracked directories refused as source.

acceptance_evidence.reference: docs/reliability/evidence/RESEARCH-601/detection-rules.md; corpus/ and corpus-2/ hold measurement.json and per-candidate candidates.jsonl with the deciding rule for every candidate; the fallback rule is chosen in the note from the corpus-2 comparison.

discovered_risks: One corpus on one machine; the share that git can decide will differ elsewhere.
27 candidates stay unresolved by design and need an explicit user override rather than a guess.
Sizes are logical lstat bytes, not allocated blocks.

evidence: Every candidate in the corpus carries its deciding rule: 986 ignored, 338 repository, 142 self-marker, 49 content, 3 manifest, 29 tracked and 27 unresolved across 47,536 directories walked.

The tracked rule runs before every other rule and refused 29 directories with output names that the repository tracks as source, including ~/localGit/echo/scripts/build and ~/localGit/disk_steward/.swiftpm. The fixture self-test asserts this case and passes 8 of 8.

1,468 of 2,615 output candidates lie outside any repository. The parent-manifest fallback resolved 20 of them and left 1,448 unresolved; self-marker and content evidence reduced that to 27, and the note states why those 27 stay unclassified rather than guessed.

Assurance reviewed: IMPACT-RESEARCH-601-BUILD, IMPACT-RESEARCH-601-ASSURANCE confirmed; INSPECT-RESEARCH-601-1 performed after the implementation event and sufficient; scope drift reconciled to those impacts; rollback is revert-only and monitoring is not applicable for a tool that does not run in the product, both recorded with the task that must replace them.

limitations: One corpus on one macOS machine; coverage of the rules elsewhere is unmeasured.
Measurement only: no product code consumes these rules until TASK-611.
The auditor also performed the research; independence rests on the archived per-candidate records and the fixture self-test.

nodes.title: Discover shared developer caches
nodes.summary: Find the shared, tool-owned caches that live outside watched project roots, present them as objects under the same contract, and keep them opt-in so the app never widens its own scope silently.

acceptance_criteria.description: Known shared caches are discovered by tool-anchored rules with stated confidence, appear as objects with size, freshness and rebuild command, require explicit opt-in before they are measured, and an unknown directory is never assumed to be a cache.

required_evidence.description: Isolated suite over fixture cache layouts plus a measured run on the maintainer corpus.

blockers: No impact records cover the audited change scope

evidence.claim: The maintainer's three watched roots hold 1,214,531 files: 888,469 inside 2,618 build-output directories totalling 65.2 GB, 37,006 inside 338 repositories totalling 4.2 GB, and 289,056 elsewhere. Treating output directories and repositories as one object each reduces the store from about 1,214,531 rows to 292,012.

Of 2,615 candidate directories, git reported 1,098 ignored and 30 tracked as source, including ~/localGit/echo/scripts/build and ~/localGit/disk_steward/.swiftpm, while 1,468 sit outside any repository. Name matching alone would have offered the 30 tracked directories for deletion.
evidence.source: git check-ignore and git ls-files over the same corpus on 2026-09-20

evidence.claim: Shared tool-owned caches outside the watched roots hold about 90 GB: ~/.cache 52 GB, ~/Library/Caches 14 GB, CoreSimulator 9.2 GB, ~/.npm 5.5 GB, pnpm 4.5 GB, DerivedData 1.9 GB and about 3.2 GB across cargo, go and gradle. None is visible to the app today.

On the installed 1.2.1 app the scan generation started 2026-09-18T11:01Z was still active on 2026-09-20T02:31Z having processed 17,365,812 entries, about fourteen times the scope, while published rows stayed at 99,977 and staged files fell from 115,309 to 22,428 between two readings. The store records 90 observation gaps and repeated retention gaps with reason database-cap-forced-eviction.
evidence.source: Read-only agent API queries against the running app on 2026-09-20

evidence.claim: The live store averages about 2,040 bytes per published row, so the 512 MiB default limit holds roughly 263,000 rows while the object model needs about 292,012 for this corpus.
evidence.source: Live store figures: 203,931,648 live bytes across 99,977 rows, 2026-09-20

decisions.question: How should build output be represented when it dominates the file count but is reproducible?
decisions.choice: Represent a build-output directory, a shared cache and a repository as one evidence object with aggregate size and no per-file rows inside it.
alternatives: Keep per-file rows and raise the storage limit to multiple gigabytes; rejected because it makes the monitor itself a large consumer and still scales with the artifact count.
Exclude build output from monitoring; rejected because it hides the largest reclaimable space, which is the product's purpose.
Sample a subset of files inside each artifact; rejected because a partial file list is neither useful for cleanup nor honest as evidence.
decisions.rationale: Artifacts are reproducible and are cleaned as a unit, so per-file provenance inside them has no user value while costing three quarters of the rows. See EV-601-CORPUS.

decisions.question: What decides that a directory is build output?
decisions.choice: Project evidence: repository ignore and tracking rules where a repository exists, manifest-anchored output locations where it does not, outermost match only, and never a tracked directory.
alternatives: Match well-known directory names; rejected because it would have offered 30 tracked source directories for deletion.
Ask the user to mark each directory; rejected as unusable at this scale, though an override remains available.
decisions.rationale: Git is decisive where present and caught real false positives; 56 percent of candidates have no repository, so a manifest fallback is required. See EV-602-GIT-ORACLE.

decisions.question: Should shared caches outside watched roots be part of the first rung?
decisions.choice: No. They form the final rung, after objects are trustworthy and visible, and they stay opt-in.
alternatives: Include them immediately; rejected because widening scope before classification is trustworthy risks presenting unreviewed deletion targets.
Leave them out entirely; rejected because they hold about 90 GB, more than the projects themselves.
decisions.rationale: Ordering keeps each rung demonstrable and keeps scope widening an explicit user choice. See EV-603-SHARED-CACHES.

decisions.question: What should happen when the configured scope cannot fit the configured limit?
decisions.choice: Refuse explicitly with the shortfall and the available remedies, and review the default limit against the object model's measured cost.
alternatives: Raise the limit silently; rejected because the user owns that trade-off.
Keep the current behaviour; rejected because it loops indefinitely while reporting healthy.
decisions.rationale: The installed app demonstrates the failure: fourteen times the scope processed with no publication and repeated forced eviction. See EV-604-STUCK-SCAN.

turning_points: Decision: Deliver four cumulative runnable increments: snapshot/export menu app; persistent evidence recorder; agent-queryable MCP integration; advanced exact provenance with fallback — Each selected rung gives the user a launchable, meaningful scenario and isolates storage, integration, and restricted-entitlement risks behind independent gates

Decision: Swift 6 with a small AppKit NSStatusItem shell, SwiftUI presentation, a shared Swift core, and SQLite persistence — The selected stack directly accesses macOS monitoring, service-management, signing, and menu APIs while minimizing continuous runtime and cross-language boundaries

turning_points: Decision: Deliver a canonical launchable Xcode app and redesigned dashboard as the first increment, then add the direct-distribution pipeline as a cumulative second increment — The first increment is independently useful and reviewable in Xcode, while Apple credential availability remains an external release dependency

Decision: Use direct distribution outside the Mac App Store under Team G3P6TU385Y with the proposed com.marudankiji.disksteward product identity — It matches the user's requested distributable desktop utility and Apple's Developer ID and notarization path; permanent identifiers also remove current configuration inconsistency

Decision: Keep the standard app complete without Endpoint Security and retain the optional extension as a separately gated target until Apple grants the restricted entitlement — This preserves the product's proven fallback while avoiding a distribution blocker and retaining the future exact-provenance path

Decision: Lead with current free-space health and a concise growth assessment, then show monitoring state and recency, with evidence export as the single clear action — This aligns the small popover with the user's immediate decision while detailed evidence remains available through export and MCP

Decision: Use one persistent Agent Access state, default off on fresh installs, that starts or stops the private local IPC service; show the state with a native toggle while keeping monitoring and manual evidence export independent — A privacy control must enforce service availability rather than merely change presentation, and it should not mutate external client configuration or interrupt the app's core evidence collection

Decision: Use a visible rolling lifecycle: 7 days of raw detail, 30 days of hourly path and capacity summaries, 365 days of daily summaries, finite anomaly detail, deterministic oldest-first pressure compaction, and a 512 MiB default hard ceiling; preserve manual exports as user-owned files and expose lifecycle status through UI and a read-only MCP tool — The tiers preserve recent forensic detail and long-term growth trends, while explicit coverage and pressure records prevent an agent from mistaking compacted history for complete history

Decision: Persist immutable observation runs and state observations, reconcile them through stable file objects and time-bounded path bindings, atomically maintain a current-file projection, and attach provenance, session context, rollups, retention, exports, and coverage gaps as separate linked records — An event chain supplies history, the materialized projection answers current state, stable identity handles rename and path reuse, and explicit observation coverage prevents unavailable roots or capped scans from fabricating deletions

Decision: Repair the existing native-app increment with one shared evidence-usefulness contract, then run two bounded branches: durable scan-generation convergence and authoritative human-triggered export; require the current-candidate gate to inspect an actual menu-created bundle from a populated database — The current database proves detailed state exists but the user path omits it, while repeated entry-cap scans cannot yet establish change history. Both defects invalidate the first actor-visible increment and can be repaired independently without changing the final intent or weakening privacy, retention, or distribution controls
